item.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

item.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

item.title: The level of cortical thickening in executive functions and audiovisual integration regions predicts reading comprehension via reading fluency in musically experienced children.
item.description:
Brain research
Proficient reading fluency, which is critical for intact reading comprehension, is related to efficient audio-visual integration and to executive functions (EF). Interestingly, musical training has been associated with better audio-visual integration, EF, and reading abilities. However, the direct relationship, cognitively and neurobiologically, between these components remains ambiguous. Here, we examined the neurobiological correlates of the predictive role of EF and audio-visual integration on reading comprehension through fluency in children with and without music experience using cortical thickness (CT) measures. A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired from 8- to 12-year-old children with and without music experience. CT within EF (anterior cingulate cortex) and audio-visual (insula) brain regions was compared between groups. A moderated mediation analysis was conducted with anterior cingulate cortex CT as the predictor variable, reading comprehension as the outcome variable, reading fluency as the mediator, and music experience as the moderator, with age and sex as covariates. Musically inexperienced children demonstrated lower reading fluency, comprehension, and EF abilities compared to experienced children. In experienced children, CT in the anterior cingulate gyrus predicted comprehension via an indirect pathway mediated by fluency (B = 21.63, BootSE = 9.11, 95 % CI [4.56, 40.85]); in inexperienced children, neither the direct nor indirect pathways significantly predicted comprehension (B = 11.53, BootSE = 8.64, 95 % CI [-6.54, 28.80]). The Index of Moderated Mediation was not significant (IMM = - 10.10, BootSE = 11.79, 95 % CI [-34.92, 12.21]); thus, there was no statistical evidence that the indirect effect differed between the groups. Results suggest that musical experience is associated with differences in neural circuits linked to EF and audiovisual integration, which in turn relate to reading fluency and comprehension.

item.title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

item.title: Immature Valence Recognition of Emotional Speech in Cochlear Implant Users: Evidence From Event-Related Potentials and Neural Oscillations.
item.description:
Ear and hearing
Objectives Rapid emotional perception in speech is crucial to efficient social communication. Cochlear implant (CI) users, constrained by device limitations in transmitting spectro-temporal detail, rely more on semantic than prosodic cues for emotional processing of spoken language. This study investigated whether CI users can rapidly recognize emotional valence based on semantic cues before full semantic comprehension when prosodic information is minimized. Design Chinese monosyllables with negative or positive valence were presented with neutral prosody using an oddball paradigm. Event-related potentials and neural oscillations were recorded in CI users and normal-hearing (NH) listeners. Results Emotional syllables evoked an N400, indicative of semantic processing, in NH listeners. Crucially, NH listeners showed an earlier mismatch negativity (MMN) for negative syllable deviants, reflecting rapid categorical perception of emotional valence. However, the N400 for positive deviants and the MMN were absent in CI users. Furthermore, compared with NH listeners, CI users showed weaker theta-band and alpha-band event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs) and inter-trial coherences and a greater beta-band ERSP. A lower beta-band ERSP was correlated with greater N400 and late negative component in NH listeners. Personality scores for extraversion and agreeableness correlated with the amplitudes of the MMN and N400 components, respectively. Conclusions The findings portray the dynamics of emotional speech processing and demonstrate that rapid recognition of emotional valence expressed by lexical meaning occurs before complete semantic processing in the NH brain. Theta activity may be associated with early emotional valence recognition, and beta activity corresponds to higher-level semantic and emotional processing. However, these two processes are immature in CI users, as evidenced by absent event-related potentials and altered neural oscillations. Personality traits may modulate emotional sensitivity, further affecting the efficiency of emotional speech processing.

item.title: Multidimensional psycholinguistic difficulty in Cantonese picture naming: Behavioral, neural, and effective connectivity evidence.
item.description:
Brain and language
Picture naming is a useful paradigm for studying spoken word production because it requires the transformation of visual object input into a lexical response through coordinated conceptual and lexical processes. This study examined whether inherent psycholinguistic difficulty in picture naming is multidimensional or unitary. Thirty-eight healthy native Cantonese speakers performed an overt object picture-naming task during fMRI. Four psycholinguistic variables were modeled: conceptual familiarity, average neighborhood distance (AND), naming disagreement, and lexical frequency. Mixed-effects models showed that higher conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency facilitated naming, whereas higher AND increased both errors and response times; naming disagreement increased errors but did not significantly affect response times. Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency on response times, indicating the facilitative effect of frequency was modulated by familiarity. For errors, significant interactions were found between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency, as well as between AND and lexical frequency, and between AND and naming disagreement, revealing complex joint influences on naming accuracy. Whole-brain analyses revealed dissociable neural effects across variables. Conjunction analysis showed that lower conceptual familiarity and higher AND converged in bilateral lateral occipital and ventral occipitotemporal regions, with extension into the left posterior temporal cortex, suggesting shared sensitivity to semantic-level difficulty. In contrast, naming disagreement and lexical frequency did not show significant lexical-level overlap. Effective connectivity analyses further identified a stable directed ROI architecture during naming. Together, the findings support a multidimensional account of picture-naming difficulty in which semantic- and lexical-related item properties impose partially distinct but interacting constraints on spoken word production.

item.title: Speech and Language Abnormalities in Putative Brain-First Versus Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
item.description:
Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
Background The α-synuclein origin model proposes brain-first and body-first Parkinson's disease (PD) subtypes, with speech potentially revealing their distinct neurodegenerative patterns. Objective We aimed to analyze the possible speech and language differences between untreated PD patients with premotor (putative body-first) and without (putative brain-first) rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Methods Speech samples of reading passages and monologues were automatically analyzed using acoustic and linguistic features. Results We enrolled 23 body-first and 35 brain-first de novo PD patients compared with 35 healthy controls. Brain-first patients showed greater speech impairment severity compared with body-first patients (P = 0.002) and controls (P < 0.001), whereas body-first patients showed greater language impairment severity compared with brain-first patients (P < 0.001) and controls (P < 0.001). Conclusions Putative brain-first subtype had more motor speech abnormalities whereas body-first subtype manifested greater language impairment. Thes finding is consistent with motor-dominant nigrostriatal involvement in brain-first and broader non-motor/cognitive involvement in body-first PD. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

item.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

item.title: Neurophysiological evidence for rapid semantic integration via fast mapping.
item.description:
Cognitive, affective & behavioral neuroscience
Theories of declarative memory consolidation hold that novel associative information is integrated into cortical semantic networks slowly and with hippocampal support. However, an encoding paradigm called fast mapping (FM) has been proposed to permit rapid cortical integration of novel item-label associations, particularly when the novel item shares substantial visual-semantic features with a simultaneously presented known concept. We tested whether associations encoded through FM immediately engage semantic memory networks, indexed by the N400 event-related potential. In contrast to behavioral semantic priming tasks, in which semantic relatedness and response congruency may be confounded, the present EEG study provides a more process-specific test of rapid semantic integration. Sixty participants encoded pairs of a novel item and an unfamiliar label under two conditions, differing with respect to the visual-semantic overlap between the novel item and a simultaneously presented known item. In a subsequent semantic priming task, the novel labels served as primes for semantically related versus unrelated targets. While behavioral results did not reveal a significant priming effect, EEG data indicated an N400 priming effect in the high-overlap FM condition, characterized by reduced N400 amplitudes for related compared with unrelated targets over a parietal electrode cluster. Crucially, the N400 effect was significantly larger after high-overlap FM than after low-overlap FM encoding, indicating that high feature overlap enhances rapid semantic integration already minutes after learning. These findings provide the first neurophysiological evidence that high-overlap FM enables rapid semantic integration.

item.title: Persistent neuroimmune alterations in children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected at age 6-7 years: Associations with language development in a South African birth cohort.
item.description:
Brain, behavior, and immunity
Background Children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected (HEU) are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental delays, yet neuroimmune pathways linking perinatal HIV exposure to school readiness remain unclear. Methods In the Drakenstein Child Health Study, 267 children (93 HEU, 174 HIV-unexposed [HU]) underwent magnetic resonance spectroscopy in midline parietal grey and left parietal white matter regions at 6-7 years. Peripheral blood serum immune markers were measured in pregnancy and in children at 6 weeks, 2, 3, and 5 years. Linear mixed-effects models characterised child immune trajectories and linear regressions tested associations with creatine-referenced neurometabolite ratios and school readiness scores. Results Mothers living with HIV had higher sCD14 and lower MMP-9, NGAL, and GM-CSF than mothers without HIV (p < 0.05). Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with altered trajectories of child sCD14, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-5, IL-10, and YKL-40. At 6-7 years, children who were HEU had lower parietal grey matter glutamate ratios and lower left parietal white matter choline ratios. By school entry, more frequent associations between child immune markers and neurometabolites were observed, with IL-8 emerging as a recurrent correlate across developmental stages. Children who were HEU had lower language scores than HU peers. Left parietal white matter choline ratios were positively associated with language and overall school readiness in HU children, but not HEU. Conclusions Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with alterations in immune development, neurometabolites reflecting both white matter maturation and neuronal health, and school readiness. Our findings highlight potential neuroimmune alterations contributing to neurodevelopmental risks in children who are HEU. A single explanatory pathway was not identified, supporting the need for longitudinal studies of neuroimmune, clinical, and environmental contributors to developmental vulnerability in this population.

item.title: Central Motor Injury as Interlayer Decoupling: An Evolutionary Information Layering Framework for Neurorehabilitation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Central motor injury is often framed as a loss of cortical command, leading rehabilitation to prioritize early cortical reactivation and active task practice. This framing captures an important part of motor impairment but leaves a second problem under-specified: how injury disrupts communication among mechanical, spinal-peripheral, and supraspinal coordination layers. The Evolutionary Information Layering (EIL) framework proposes that biological coordination develops through the retention, specialization, and integration of ancestral regulatory systems rather than through their replacement. Applying EIL to neurorehabilitation, this article conceptualizes severe central motor injury as interlayer decoupling, defined here as a loss of phase-, context-, and task-appropriate conditional influence among functional layers. Three interacting disturbances are proposed: reduced reliability of descending commands, maladaptive gain from residual descending activity, and preserved but insufficiently engaged lower-layer mechanical and spinal coordination. Rehabilitation can therefore be organized as layer reweighting rather than as competition between cortical and spinal mechanisms. The therapeutic sequence is to titrate premature higher-layer demand, re-engage structured lower-layer information, and progressively reintegrate higher-level predictive control. The framework generates testable predictions concerning phase-dependent spinal modulation, proximal coordination, and task-specific cortical engagement. It also provides a theoretical basis for lower-layer-informed rehabilitation protocols without claiming that spinal circuits replace cortical function. Because most indirect evidence comes from stroke and human locomotor or spinal cord studies, application to traumatic brain injury and other central nervous system disorders should remain diagnosis-dependent.

item.title: Children with developmental language disorder show selective impairments in low-frequency neural tracking of speech.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Neural tracking of slow temporal modulations in speech supports extraction of the prosodic and syllabic structure thought to be critical for language acquisition by Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, yet whether these automatic cortical tracking mechanisms are altered in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) remains unclear. We recorded MEG while children with and without DLD listened to a story, and quantified source-level lagged speech-brain coherence and frequency-specific cortical functional connectivity across bilateral cortical regions. As expected a priori by TS theory, children with DLD showed significantly reduced coherence in the 0.9-2.5 Hz range associated with prosodic information in the story, spanning bilateral auditory and speech-related cortex. The strongest regional group differences were in left supramarginal gyrus (p < 0.001) and right inferior frontal gyrus (p = 0.001). In the 2.5-5 Hz range, linked to syllabic-rate modulations in the story, children with DLD showed reduced coherence in right temporal regions (all p < 0.02). Stronger low-frequency speech-brain coherence was associated with better language performance, indicating that individual differences in cortical speech tracking were behaviourally meaningful. No reliable differences were observed at higher modulation rates (5-9 Hz or 12-40 Hz). Exploratory functional connectivity analyses did not reveal network-level group differences that were robust across ROI time-series extraction methods. These findings indicate that atypical low-frequency neural tracking of speech is functionally relevant to language outcomes in DLD.

item.title: Developmental Aspects of Language Mapping with Stereoelectroencephalography.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
Summary This review examines developmental perspectives on the use of stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) for delineating language areas and networks in pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, both as a clinical tool for presurgical evaluation and as a modality for gaining neuroscientific insights into speech and language development. Language development is a dynamic process that begins before birth and continues into adulthood, shaped by the maturation of brain networks. SEEG allows high-resolution study of these networks, providing a unique perspective on the organization of language systems. This review traces language acquisition from early infancy through adolescence and adulthood, highlighting the pivotal role of neural oscillations. We then summarize classical and contemporary neural models of language organization, highlighting the distributed and hierarchical networks, and emphasize the high spatial and temporal resolution of SEEG for presurgical planning that enables clinicians to optimize neurosurgical interventions while preserving essential language areas and the tracts connecting them. Our review also addresses the human brain's remarkable plasticity and capacity for reorganization, which are especially pronounced in children and vital for adaptation to and recovery from neurologic injury or surgery. We focus specifically on developmental reorganization in pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and its implications for language mapping with SEEG. The review concludes with recommendations for designing language-mapping batteries tailored to the unique needs of pediatric patients.

item.title: The role of semantically related co-speech gestures in English-to-Chinese consecutive interpreting: a behavioral and ERP study.
item.description:
Acta psychologica
Co-speech gestures are an important source of visual-semantic information in communication, yet how the semantic relatedness of speech and gesture influences both comprehension and production during consecutive interpreting (CI) remains insufficiently understood. To this end, the present study combined behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) measure to examine how semantically related and semantically unrelated co-speech gestures affect source-language comprehension and target-language production in English-to-Chinese CI through a cue-recall task and oral translation. The comprehension-related results showed that gesture condition did not significantly affect cue-recall accuracy, but semantically related gestures were associated with faster responses than semantically unrelated gestures. ERP results during real-time comprehension further showed that semantically related gestures elicited less negative N400 amplitudes, which were distributed along the anterior-posterior scalp axis and maximal over parietal sites. The production-related results showed translation scores were also higher in the semantically related gesture condition. These effects remained stable after verbal working memory was included as a covariate. Overall, the findings provide initial behavioral and neurocognitive evidence that co-speech gestures are integrated with speech during CI, and that reduced semantic relatedness between speech and gesture increases online semantic processing demands with downstream consequences for target-language production. The study advances a multimodal account of consecutive interpreting by showing that visually available co-speech gestures shape both source-language comprehension and subsequent target-language production.

item.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

item.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

item.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

item.title: Cross-Condition Transfer Learning for EEG-Based Inner Speech Classification: A Controlled Evaluation of Neural Networks and Temporal Segmentation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Transferring a decoder trained on overt (pronounced) speech to inner speech has been proposed to offset scarce inner-speech EEG. This was re-examined on the “Thinking out loud” dataset (ds003626, 10 participants, four words), with no test trial in training or selection. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, CSP+LDA and a Riemannian tangent-space pipeline were compared on bidirectional transfer, combined training, overt pre-training with fine-tuning on 25–100% inner-speech subsets, maximum-mean-discrepancy alignment and four trial windows. Shuffled-label controls and an exploratory, post hoc test family were used. Cross-participant, held-out-session, channel, band, external-electrode and second-dataset (ds006104) arms were reference checks. Within participant, overt speech was decodable in the action interval (0.34–0.43, chance 0.250). It survived a held-out session, peaked in 30–100 Hz and did not cross participants. Two lip electrodes alone decoded the pronounced word at 0.67–0.83. Regressing the external electrodes out of the scalp reduced three decoders’ overt accuracy to 0.28–0.40, leaving a residual of undetermined origin. Inner-speech accuracy was not distinguishable from chance. No transfer method, fine-tuned or not, improved reliably on its controls. Effects below about 2–6 percentage points were likely missed. These findings suggest that articulation-related features learned from overt speech may not provide sufficiently transferable information for inner-speech decoding under the present conditions.

item.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions.Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

item.title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning.Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

item.title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual "cocktail-party" paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding-decoding analyses. Participants (18 females, 14 males) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated midlatency (100-250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270-450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory-language processing during selective listening of continuous speech.

item.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. Methods In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. Results Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). Semantic processing was highly specific but insensitive for predicting both recovery of consciousness (specificity 94%, sensitivity 18%) and functional recovery (specificity 92%, sensitivity 29%). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. Discussion EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Posterior-lateral basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei hypoconnectivity in the inferior frontal cortex is associated with verbal fluency deficits in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia (Heidelberg, Germany)
Cognitive impairment is a core feature of schizophrenia and remains insufficiently addressed by current treatments. Increasing evidence implicates the cholinergic system, particularly the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei (BFCN), in cognitive dysfunction. While structural alterations of the BFCN have been reported, alterations in their intrinsic functional connectivity (iFC) remain unclear. The present study examined the iFC of anterior and posterior BFCN subdivisions (aBFCN, pBFCN) in schizophrenia and tested associations with cognitive performance. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from the COBRE dataset were analyzed, including 73 healthy controls (HC) and 51 patients with schizophrenia (SCZ). Seed-based connectivity analyses were performed for aBFCN and pBFCN. Group differences were assessed voxel-wise, and group-dependent associations with phonemic verbal fluency (FAS) and processing speed (BACS-SC) were tested using hierarchical regression controlling for age, sex, IQ, and smoking status; verbal learning and memory (HVLT) was examined as a specificity analysis. Exploratory molecular mapping used normative PET-derived neurotransmitter maps, supplemented by spatial-autocorrelation-preserving null models. Distinct connectivity patterns of aBFCN and pBFCN were observed, consistent with previous reports in HC. Compared with HC, SCZ showed reduced pBFCN connectivity with a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis; BA44; p = 0.018, FWE-corrected), whereas no significant differences were observed for aBFCN. The Group × pBFCN-IFG connectivity interaction was significant for FAS (p = 0.014) but not BACS-SC (p = 0.762) or HVLT (p = 0.514). In SCZ, higher pBFCN-IFG connectivity was associated with better FAS performance. Descriptive molecular mapping showed above-average representation of M1 and α4β2 receptor maps as well as several non-cholinergic targets; however, no molecular target showed significant spatial correspondence after spatial-autocorrelation-aware testing and FDR correction. These findings provide evidence for selective pBFCN hypoconnectivity with the right inferior frontal gyrus in schizophrenia. Its association with verbal fluency suggests that disrupted pBFCN connectivity with the inferior frontal cortex may contribute to altered executive control processes involved in verbal fluency in schizophrenia. Together, these findings extend previous evidence of BFCN abnormalities in schizophrenia by demonstrating a systems-level functional alteration of pBFCN-cortical connectivity and its relationship with cognitive performance.

item.title: Decoupling language and emotion in the bilingual brain.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
In a recent article, Davydova et al. showed that affect labeling fails in a second, less-proficient language due to the amygdala-ventrolateral prefrontal cortex functional connectivity. This subcortical decoupling also explains the emotional blunting that bilinguals report when using their less-proficient language.

item.title: Orthographic repetition elicits enhancement without suppression at both the word- and character-levels in Chinese.
item.description:
International journal of psychophysiology : official journal of the International Organization of Psychophysiology
In Chinese, orthographic repetition (e.g., ""-"") modulates neural activity associated with orthographic processing around 200 ms after target onset, as indexed by the N200 enhancement effect. The present study combined time-frequency analysis with priming paradigms in two EEG experiments to determine whether orthographic repetition is accompanied by oscillatory power enhancement or suppression. In Experiment 1, complete repetition priming of two-character words elicited both a significant N200 enhancement effect and significant theta power enhancement relative to the control condition, whereas no significant N200 or theta-power enhancement was detected for semantic or phonological priming. To separate orthographic overlap from the concomitant phonological and semantic repetition inherent in complete repetition, Experiment 2 used partial orthographic repetition with single-character prime-target pairs that differed in phonology and semantics and replicated both effects. Exploratory participant-level correlations between the N200 and total theta effects were positive but nonsignificant in both experiments. A positive correlation between N200 enhancement and evoked theta enhancement reached the unadjusted significance threshold only in Experiment 2. These findings indicate that orthographic repetition is associated with enhancement rather than suppression of theta-band activity and that this pattern extends across word and character levels.

item.title: Candidate Magnetic Resonance Imaging Biomarkers of Language Recovery in Post-Stroke Aphasia: A Framework for Future Acupuncture-Response Prediction.
item.description:
Journal of visualized experiments : JoVE
Language recovery after post-stroke aphasia (PSA) shows substantial interindividual variability, creating a need for objective markers that can characterize recovery potential and support individualized rehabilitation. This narrative review synthesizes magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evidence relevant to language recovery and rehabilitation response in PSA, including structural MRI, diffusion MRI, functional MRI, and multimodal imaging. Existing studies indicate that lesion characteristics, white-matter integrity, regional functional activity, functional connectivity, and dynamic network organization are associated with aphasia severity, subsequent language recovery, or response to conventional rehabilitation. Multimodal approaches integrating imaging with clinical and behavioral information may provide a more comprehensive representation of individual recovery potential. Given the growing interest in applying neuroimaging to individualized acupuncture rehabilitation for PSA, an important question is whether these recovery-related MRI features can also inform acupuncture-response prediction. However, these findings primarily concern general prognosis or conventional rehabilitation outcomes and should not be interpreted as evidence of acupuncture-specific responsiveness. Acupuncture-related neuroimaging studies have mainly characterized treatment-associated changes in brain activity and functional connectivity rather than prospectively testing whether pretreatment MRI features predict individual treatment response. Accordingly, these MRI findings are better regarded as candidate imaging features for future acupuncture-response research than as validated predictors of acupuncture-specific benefit. We therefore propose a hypothesis-driven framework in which multimodal MRI is integrated with clinical and treatment information and evaluated within prospective controlled designs to distinguish general recovery potential from additional benefit attributable to acupuncture. Rigorous model development, external validation, and prospective testing will be required before imaging-based approaches can be considered for individualized acupuncture-response stratification.

item.title: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear. Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper. Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084). Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

item.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

item.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and language development: biological evidence from an integrative review.
item.description:
Developmental neurorehabilitation
Objective This study aimed to analyze scientific evidence on the relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and its potential implications for language development and speech fluency. Methods An integrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases between August 2025 and July 2026. The search strategy included terms related to vitamin B12, myelination, brain development, language, and speech. Original studies published in English investigating the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency on the central nervous system, neurodevelopment, or structural brain changes were included. Results Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were synthesized through thematic narrative analysis. The findings indicated a relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and delayed neuropsychomotor development, impaired myelination, reduced white matter integrity, and structural brain abnormalities identified by neuroimaging. Furthermore, studies investigating the neural circuits underlying language showed that these same structures are essential for language organization and speech fluency, providing biological plausibility for a potential relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and impairments in these processes. Conclusion Vitamin B12 deficiency may adversely affect neurodevelopment and cerebral myelination, representing a potential mechanism underlying alterations in the maturation of neural circuits involved in language. These findings support the biological plausibility that vitamin B12 deficiency may contribute to impaired language development through disrupted cerebral myelination, although direct clinical evidence remains lacking.

item.title: Audio large language models align with human neural responses during spoken-language comprehension.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Audio large language models (audio LLMs) process continuous speech directly and transform it into progressively more abstract representations, providing a useful computational point of comparison with human spoken-language comprehension. Previous studies have reported model-brain correspondence for pretrained speech models and text-based language models, but it remains unclear which internal representations of audio LLMs are most closely associated with neural responses during online listening. We compared EEG responses from 41 native Mandarin listeners with internal representations from Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Kimi-Audio in a Mandarin auditory semantic-violation paradigm that controlled sentence structure and event boundaries. We extracted speech-related and word-level semantic-update representations and quantified their incremental contributions to held-out EEG prediction beyond lower-level controls. Audio LLM representations improved EEG prediction beyond the acoustic envelope, phoneme onsets, and word onsets (Δr = 0.012, corrected P = 0.028). Prediction-score partitioning indicated that semantic violation primarily increased the overlap in EEG-predictive information between speech-related and semantic-update representations, rather than the unique contribution of either representation class. This pattern was relatively stable in Qwen2-Audio and Qwen2.5-Omni and directionally consistent, although statistically weaker, in Kimi-Audio. These findings provide component-level evidence that audio-conditioned model representations correspond to human neural responses during spoken-language comprehension, without implying mechanistic equivalence.

item.title: Differentiating language-specific from language-related network dynamics using dynamic functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Cognitive neurodynamics
Language processing is a highly complex dynamic neural activity that requires the recruitment of both regions critical for language processing and large-scale cognitive networks. Because language networks are interconnected and dynamically reconfigure their connections depending on task demand and complexity, it is challenging to differentiate language-specific networks form language-related cognitive networks during both resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) and task-based fMRI (tb-fMRI). Prior evidence demonstrated state-dependent differences in dynamic functional connectivity (FC) within identical networks across rest- and task-conditions. Based on this evidence, we hypothesized that examining dynamic FC patterns could help differentiate the functional specialization of large-scale neural networks in the human brain. Thus, we examined whether temporal patterns of dynamic FC could functionally differentiate networks engaged during a language task. Using a data-driven dynamic FC framework, we tested whether rest-task state transitions preferentially modulate subsets of large-scale networks. Specifically, we examined whether monotonic temporal trends in dynamic FC, used as a first-order approximation of sustained task engagement, were more prominent in networks showing task-sensitive dynamics, while others exhibited resting-state-like dynamics. We analyzed rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI data from 172 healthy participants (86 females, 27.6 ± 3.8 years old) from the Human Connectome Project. Dynamic FC analyses revealed significant state-dependent differences in correlation variability between rs-fMRI and tb-fMRI (Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.001). A subset of networks exhibited task-sensitive temporal modulation, whereas other networks showed dynamic patterns closely paralleled resting-like dynamics without reaching statistical significance. These findings suggest that dynamic FC provides a useful framework for functionally distinguishing language-specific networks from language-related cognitive networks. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10579-0.

item.title: Aphasic status epilepticus presenting with prominent psychiatric symptoms: A case report.
item.description:
PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Background Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is a subtype of nonconvulsive status epilepticus characterized by aphasia as its primary ictal manifestation. Although psychiatric symptoms are uncommon in ASE, they may obscure the diagnosis when present. We report an atypical case, presenting predominantly with agitation and irritability, which was rapidly diagnosed as ASE by electroencephalography (EEG) based on the abrupt symptom onset and neurological history. Case presentation A 49-year-old right-handed woman with alcohol use disorder was referred to our psychiatric hospital because of agitation, irritability, and disorganized thinking. Approximately 2 months before presentation to our hospital, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 days after sustaining a head injury. A left posterior fossa subdural hematoma was diagnosed, and burr-hole evacuation was performed at a general hospital. She continued rehabilitation; however, 6 days before admission to our hospital, she suddenly developed incoherent speech with agitation and irritability, prompting referral to our psychiatric hospital. Neurological examination revealed sensory aphasia. Given the history of brain injury and abrupt symptom onset, EEG was performed and demonstrated left-dominant periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges, confirming ASE. Antiseizure treatment resolved the EEG abnormalities and aphasia; however, aphasia, agitation, and irritability recurred with periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges. The symptoms improved with intravenous diazepam, and no recurrence was observed for >2 years following optimization of antiseizure medication. Conclusion ASE may present predominantly with psychiatric symptoms and be misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder. Recognizing symptom chronology and epileptogenic background is essential for prompting EEG evaluation and early diagnosis.

item.title: Human medial frontal neurons represent integrated semantic content and sensory evidence to inform decision-making
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans can reconfigure how they act on the world from a single verbal instruction. Central to this capacity is the ability to represent what an instruction specifies and to bring that content to bear on incoming sensory evidence. However, little is known about where in the human brain instruction content is encoded, how it combines with sensory evidence to produce a choice, and how this integration relates to behavior. Here, we characterized single-neuron and population responses recorded in the ventral temporal cortex, medial temporal lobe, medial frontal cortex and ventro-medial prefrontal cortex of neurosurgical patients performing a verbal instruction task. On each trial, a written instruction specified which stimulus feature was relevant and whether the correct response was to choose or to reject the stimulus that best matched it, so that the same image pair required opposite responses under different instructions. Only medial frontal populations jointly encoded the instructed task, and the target feature, whereas ventral temporal populations encoded stimulus features along axes that generalized across instruction conditions. Choice representation emerged first in ventromedial prefrontal and then in medial frontal cortex during stimulus presentation, before a motor response could be prepared. Shuffling instruction content selectively degraded prediction of medial frontal population activity, whereas shuffling stimulus identity selectively degraded ventral temporal activity. To ask how these representations could be computed, we trained a vision-language model with separable visual and linguistic streams converging on a recurrent decision module to perform the same task. Its visual embeddings predicted held-out ventral temporal activity and its recurrent activations revealed a task solution space that predicted medial frontal activity, and the strength of this alignment tracked behavioral accuracy. These results identify a cortical hierarchy in which medial frontal circuitry represents the content of verbal goals and acts on a ventral temporal substrate whose representational axes remain stable, and indicate that functional hierarchies discovered in artificial networks can serve as predictive models of human neural circuitry.

item.title: Pre- and postnatal environmental lithium exposure and adolescent neurodevelopment: a tooth-biomarker study
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Lithium is a naturally occurring element found in drinking water, and its environmental presence is rising with demand for batteries. Yet evidence on lithium comes almost entirely from adults, ecological studies, or medical treatment, leaving the effects of prenatal and early postnatal environmental exposure unknown. We laser-mapped lithium in shed baby teeth, which preserve a record of exposure around birth (-12 to +13 weeks), from 448 U.S. youth in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and tested associations with brain structure, cognition, and behavior at ages 9-10. Higher lithium was found in children of less-educated caregivers and from more deprived neighborhoods. Higher lithium was also linked to thicker cortices, varying surface area, mostly smaller subcortical volumes, poorer reading and language ability, and more externalizing problems, with associations varying by caregiver education. Early-life environmental lithium exposure may therefore be socioeconomically patterned and contribute to disparities in neurodevelopment, warranting environmental health surveillance.

item.title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x106 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x104 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x104 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates.Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

item.title: Beyond the cortex, early deficits, late recovery: a systematic review of language outcomes and subcortical mapping after awake craniotomy for diffuse gliomas.
item.description:
Chinese neurosurgical journal
Background To evaluate immediate and long-term postoperative language outcomes in patients undergoing awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation (DES) for diffuse gliomas in eloquent regions. Methods PRISMA-compliant systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261342690) of adults (≥ 18 years) with supratentorial diffuse glioma in the language-dominant hemisphere enrolled in both randomised and non-randomised studies of awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation and language mapping. Databases searched included PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL (from 2010 to March 2026). Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by multiple reviewers using standardised tools (JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists). Due to methodological heterogeneity, narrative synthesis was performed. Results Ten studies (532 patients enrolled; 55.3% male) published 2011-2025 were included; tumour grade was reported inconsistently, with higher-grade tumours predominating in the larger cohorts and at least 114 patients having WHO grade 4 disease. Early postoperative deficits ranged from 2.2 to 100% depending on assessment timing and measure (immediate post-op: up to 100%; day 7 to week 1: 2.2-22%). Persistent deficits at ≥ 3 months ranged from 0 to 47%. In three studies reporting whole-cohort outcomes with standardised assessment, rates were 0-5.6%. Papagno et al., using 3-month cut-offs, found that 47% of patients with uncinate fasciculus resection had impairment in famous face naming versus 10% with the tract preserved. The general trend was early decline followed by improvement, with most reported deficits resolving by around 3 months. Heterogeneous deficit definitions and inconsistent baseline assessment preclude treating this as a prognostic pattern, and resections involving the uncinate fasciculus were a notable outlier, underscoring the need for systematic subcortical tract mapping. Conclusion Awake craniotomy with DES remains the gold standard for preserving language. Early deficits are common but predominantly transient, and reported deficit rates appear closely associated with the timing of assessment. Persistent deficits assessed at ≥ 3 months were low in most studies, although rates varied considerably with the outcome measure used and with subcortical tract involvement. Subcortical tract involvement warrants systematic mapping. We advocate for the global adoption of standardised perioperative linguistic protocols to improve data comparability. Systematic review registration PROSPERO CRD420261342690.

item.title: Association of bilingual language use with brain age: MRI evidence from bilinguals, translators, and interpreters.
item.description:
Neuroimage. Reports
Background Bilingualism has been linked to cognitive reserve and later onset of Mild Cognitive Impairment, but its neuroanatomical correlates remain unclear. We examined whether structural MRI-derived brain age varies across bilingual groups with different professional language experience. Objective To test whether brain age differs among non-professional bilinguals, translators, and simultaneous interpreters. Methods We included 105 Czech-English bilingual adults (44 non-professional bilinguals, 35 translators, 26 simultaneous interpreters). Brain age was estimated using six pretrained models. The primary outcome was the age-corrected brain-age gap (BAGcorr ). Group differences and age × group interactions were tested across models with FDR correction. Prediction accuracy and residual age dependence were also characterised. The model showing the largest standardised BAGcorr group effect was taken forward for exploratory post hoc age-slope and regional-volume analyses. Results No group difference in BAGcorr survived FDR correction across the six models. No age × group interaction survived correction, although nominal interactions were observed for BrainAge and DeepBrainNet. Model-quality criteria ranked the models differently, with no single model consistently preferred. In BrainAge, the sex- and ICV-adjusted BAGcorr difference between interpreters and non-professional bilinguals was -1.61 years (95% CI: -3.66 to 0.44). Exploratory age-slope and regional-volume associations were model-specific and did not provide robust evidence of group differences. Conclusions Professional bilingual experience was not robustly associated with age-corrected brain-age gap across pretrained models. Brain-age inference was sensitive to model choice and age-bias correction. BrainAge-specific interpreter patterns should therefore be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of a general difference in biological brain ageing.

item.title: What can functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography reveal about the cerebral lateralization of writing.
item.description:
FEBS letters
Written language is central to modern life, yet its cerebral lateralization remains far less understood than that of oral language. This review synthesizes evidence from five functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD) studies (n = 268; 228 adults and 40 children aged 7-9 years), a method well-suited to studying writing due to its tolerance of natural movement. The linguistic component of writing has been shown to be left-lateralized in right-handers, mirroring oral language, whereas for left-handers findings remain inconclusive. Linguistic processing appears largely independent of whether words are produced by hand or keyboard. The unresolved issue is dissociating linguistic from motor components as writing movements may themselves be intrinsically linguistic. Future research should address underexplored populations and leverage writing as a model for neuroplasticity.
